content: The first type, primary hypertension, occurs without any underlying medical condition and is often idiopathic in nature. The second type, secondary hypertension, arises as a result of another medical condition. Conditions that can lead to secondary hypertension include kidney disease, adrenal gland disorders, hyperparathyroidism, thyroid dysfunction, coarctation of the aorta, and obstructive sleep apnea. In many cases, hypertension is asymptomatic, meaning it does not present with noticeable symptoms. Several factors increase the risk of developing hypertension. These include advancing age, genetic predisposition (family history), race, being overweight or obese, tobacco use, a diet high in sodium or low in potassium, diabetes, physical inactivity, and chronic stress. If left uncontrolled, hypertension can lead to severe complications. These include myocardial infarction (heart attack) or cerebrovascular accidents (strokes), the formation of aneurysms, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, vision impairment, peripheral artery disease, hypertensive crises, and sexual dysfunction.
